questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Define a social movement and separate it from a narrow campaign
questions.stem: Ticket COMP-118 asks the team to describe what distinguishes a social movement from a single-issue pressure campaign.

options.text: A social movement mobilizes sustained, organized support across a broad constituency to pursue shared goals.
A social movement is any group that sends letters to officials about one issue at least once a year.
options.misconception: treats any organised letter campaign as a movement

options.text: A social movement requires the formal registration of a party with the national electoral commission.
options.misconception: assumes a movement must register as a political party

options.text: A social movement is best identified by how much media coverage it attracts during its first week.
options.misconception: judges a movement mainly by media attention

questions.explanation: A movement is sustained collective mobilisation toward shared goals. The distractors confuse a one-off campaign with organisation, and treat party registration or media coverage as the decisive test.
questions.hint: Think about durability and breadth, not paperwork.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what an election management authority is responsible for
questions.stem: Ticket OPS-207 asks why the national election office publishes voter lists, funds polling stations and staffs the count itself.

options.text: Elections are managed so that the result is accepted as legitimate by every party involved.
options.misconception: thinks management only favours the incumbent

options.text: Elections are managed mainly to create a professional career path for permanent election staff.
options.misconception: believes management exists mainly to staff careers

options.text: Elections are managed so every eligible voter can register and cast a ballot under agreed rules.
Elections are managed because parliaments lack the constitutional power to oversee the count itself.
options.misconception: reads management as a constitutional power grab

questions.explanation: Managed elections place registration, polling and counting under one authority so rules stay predictable. The distractors reduce it to incumbent advantage, staffing perks or constitutional conflict.
questions.hint: Ask who benefits from rule-bound administration.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Justify the use of penalties for refusing to vote
questions.stem: Ticket GOV-314 asks the team to argue why the state should keep fines for citizens who refuse to go to the polls.

answer.exemplar: A fine is defensible because compulsory voting corrects the classic underrepresentation of the poor, the young and the apathetic: when non-voting is costless, those with the most free time and political interest dominate, and elected officials then answer to a narrow slice of citizens. The fine also treats the ballot as a civic duty similar to jury service, which stabilises majorities and reduces the temptation of parties to ignore broad but low-participation constituencies. The justification still requires exemptions for illness and hardship, independent oversight of the roll, and a genuine uncontested ballot for the rule to remain legitimate.

questions.explanation: A defensible case rests on correcting skewed participation and on civic duty. The tempting alternative, that fines punish the poor, ignores exemptions and oversight that can address hardship.
questions.hint: Focus on who is missing from the electorate.

options.misconception: assumes groups must stay clear of parties

options.misconception: assumes endorsement bans explain group abstention

options.text: Interest groups shape policy where they matter, but only parties win office and make government accountable.

questions.explanation: Interest groups shape policy but cannot hold office, so they still need parties. The distractors mistake successful lobbying for electoral irrelevance, or invent a legal bar that was never given.
questions.hint: Ask who can actually be voted out of office.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret the electoral effect of concentrated media coverage

options.text: The effect is limited because most voters in the region admit they rarely read the daily newspaper.
options.misconception: assumes low readership cancels the effect of coverage

options.text: The effect is limited because the scandal concerns funding rules rather than the candidate's competence.
options.misconception: assumes voters separate scandals from competence

options.text: The effect will favour whichever party can afford to buy the widest circulation in the region.
options.misconception: assumes coverage simply reflects advertising spend

questions.explanation: Agenda-setting means concentrated coverage can push one issue onto voters' priorities. The distractors understate attention and treat coverage as bought or competence-only.
questions.hint: Think about what the coverage makes voters talk about.

questions.learningObjective: Compare how district magnitude shapes party competition
questions.stem: Ticket GEO-705 compares two identical city districts, one electing a single member and the other electing five members.

options.text: The five-member district is more competitive because more candidates must stand to fill the seats.
options.misconception: thinks more seats in a district add competition

options.misconception: thinks party slates increase voter choice

options.misconception: assumes competitiveness depends only on voter numbers

options.misconception: thinks observers appoint the polling supervisors

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Account for the reasons a post-election coalition collapses
questions.stem: Ticket GOV-901 asks the team to account for why a coalition formed after an election can collapse without any formal dissolution vote.

answer.exemplar: A post-election coalition is a negotiated bundle of policies, offices and confidence measures, so it can fail without any single breach of law. Members may find the deal's costs, such as spending limits, ministerial portfolios or reform timetables, harder to absorb once ministries begin operating, and a partner may judge that the governing arithmetic is shifting against it. Parties also face internal discipline from members who promised a different settlement. The right account therefore combines renegotiation attempts, cabinet disagreements over policy and defections to the opposition, rather than attributing collapse to one dramatic betrayal or to a legal dissolution procedure.

questions.explanation: Collapse usually comes from renegotiating portfolios and policy plus internal party discipline, not a legal event. The tempting story of one traitor misses the continuing bargain behind government.
questions.hint: Look for negotiation, not one dramatic event.

questions.explanation: Mobilization needs time to fix logistics and find hesitant voters. The distractors reframe the failure as volunteer numbers, settled intentions or a candidate's calendar.
questions.hint: Focus on time available to solve last-minute problems.

questions.stem: Ticket VOT-1301 asks the team to assess the claim that compulsory voting made turnout more equal between wealthy and poor districts.

options.text: The claim is implausible because turnout figures never vary between districts of different incomes.
options.misconception: assumes turnout is identical across income groups

The claim is implausible because poor districts already vote at higher rates than wealthy ones.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Weigh the claim that interest groups have made parties redundant
questions.stem: Ticket GRP-1410 asks the team to weigh the claim that well-organised interest groups have made political parties redundant.

answer.exemplar: Interest groups do not make parties redundant because the two perform different functions. Groups use information, money and publicity to shape the content of policy within a narrow domain, and they are usually free to ignore the electoral costs of their demands. Parties, by contrast, contest every constituency, assemble coalitions across issues and regions, and must offer voters a prospect of collective reward for supporting them, including the promise that somebody will be held responsible for government performance. A group that wins a policy concession has usually done so by bargaining with parties that then need that support to build a majority, so the group's success depends on the party's continued electoral strength rather than replacing it.

questions.explanation: Groups shape policy within a domain; parties contest every seat and offer collective accountability. The tempting conclusion ignores that victories depend on bargaining with parties that need them.
questions.hint: Compare the two institutions' different functions.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate registration drives as a route to sustained turnout
questions.stem: Ticket GOT-2007 asks the team to evaluate the claim that registering residents of an underserved district will, on its own, produce sustained turnout.

answer.exemplar: Registration is a necessary but weak lever: it removes the barrier of not being on the roll, but it does not supply a reason to vote on the day. Sustained participation in under-served areas usually requires repeated contact, sometimes in the language or venue that residents already use, plus organisations trusted locally to remind people on the day itself. A registration drive run once by a distant party produces a larger roll and often no change in turnout, because the marginal registrants are precisely those least attached to politics, and newly registered non-voters may even depress the average turnout rate. The team should therefore expect registration to raise the ceiling on participation while relying on other tools for the floor.

questions.explanation: Registration expands the pool but supplies no motivation on polling day, so marginal registrants stay inactive. The tempting claim that a bigger roll means higher turnout ignores new entries.
questions.hint: Distinguish eligibility from willingness to vote.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the main reason the electoral authority publishes a pre-election list
questions.stem: Ticket ADM-2205 asks the team to state the main reason electoral authorities publish a pre-election voter list.

answer.exemplar: The pre-election list is published so that parties, candidates and voters can check who is registered before polling day, and so that disputed entries can be corrected in time to matter. It also standardises the roll from which turnout will later be calculated, giving a common reference point for observers and for results verification. Publishing it several weeks ahead is what makes challenge possible at all, because once a name is missing from the roll the voter's opportunity to vote may already have been lost. The list is therefore a transparency and correction device first, and an administrative artefact second.

questions.explanation: Publishing the list allows correction before polling and standardises the roll used for turnout. The tempting alternative, that it is a formality, misses that correction needs an advance public list.
questions.hint: What does publication make possible before polling?

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Weigh the argument that enlarging constituencies improves representation
questions.stem: Ticket DSP-2707 asks the team to weigh the argument that enlarging constituencies always improves the quality of representation.

answer.exemplar: Enlarging constituencies does not reliably improve representation; it redistributes the trade-off between proportionality and local accountability. In single-member districts a larger seat raises the threshold for entry, so a party need only organise in one part of a bigger area to win it, and a party with a scattered base can be shut out entirely even where it is locally strong. Where the electoral system is proportional or uses multi-member seats, larger districts are more likely to smooth out vote-to-seat distortions and make the seat-to-vote ratio more uniform, so the effect depends on the system rather than on size alone. The defensible conclusion is that size is a parameter to be set against the system, and that a blanket rule of always enlarging has no general basis.

questions.explanation: Seat size trades proportionality against entry costs and local accountability, and its effect depends on the system. The tempting rule that bigger is always better ignores the single-member threshold.
questions.hint: Ask which system the seats belong to.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a flat rate penalty for failing to vote
questions.stem: Ticket VOTE-3303 asks the team to evaluate a proposal that the fine for failing to vote be set at one flat rate for all citizens.

answer.exemplar: A flat fine is defensible only if the rule is enforced without discretion and if genuine obstacles are excused rather than priced out. A flat rate treats voting as a civic obligation of equal force on everyone, which protects the idea that participation is not a privilege of the comfortable. It also avoids the temptation, created by graduated fines, of deciding in advance that some citizens' time is worth more than others, a judgement that would import income differences into the franchise itself. The scheme then requires a clear, uniform process for hardship exemptions, published enforcement statistics, and a fine small enough that it does not deter a poor citizen from voting, otherwise the flat rate simply replaces exclusion with a heavier penalty.

questions.explanation: A flat fine preserves the equal-citizen logic of the franchise if enforcement is uniform and hardship is excused. The tempting fairness objection ignores that graduated fines judge citizens' worth.
questions.hint: Ask what a graduated fine would take as an input.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State which electoral systems most often use a second round
questions.stem: Ticket R2-3609 asks the team to state which kinds of electoral system most commonly make use of a second round.

answer.exemplar: A second round is most common where the law requires an outright majority rather than a plurality, and presidential elections are the clearest case, with the top two candidates contesting a final after no one reaches the threshold. Some legislative elections use the same device for a directly elected presidency of parliament or for a tie. The mechanism is chosen because it gives a clear winner with majority support, at the cost of two campaigns and the possibility of strategic alliances between the first and second placed candidates. A second round is not a synonym for preferential voting, where the single ballot already allows ranked choices, and it is not part of proportional allocation, where seats are computed from the national vote.

questions.explanation: A second round is used where the law demands an outright majority, most often in presidential elections. The distractors confuse preferential counting, plurality and proportional allocation.
questions.hint: Think about what the law demands, not the counting method.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Weigh whether a movement's decline disproves its demands
questions.stem: Ticket MOV-4108 asks the team to weigh the argument that a movement's decline proves its demands were unjustified.

answer.exemplar: A movement's decline does not prove its demands were unjustified, because organisational survival and the validity of a claim are different things. Movements commonly exhaust themselves after achieving a symbolic or partial concession, when the coalition of convenience that held the organisation together dissolves; a state may also absorb a demand by co-opting the leadership or by enacting a diluted version that splits the movement. A movement can therefore fade while its central claim is later vindicated, as when a rights framework is adopted years after the campaign that first proposed it. The defensible conclusion is that decline is evidence about the organisation's strategy and the regime's response, and only weak indirect evidence about the merit of the claim itself.

questions.explanation: Decline reflects exhaustion, co-option or dilution, not the merit of a claim. The tempting inference mistakes organisational fate for a verdict on the issue.
questions.hint: Separate an organisation's fate from a claim's merit.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Weigh the claim that a new single-member district is more competitive
questions.stem: Ticket DLG-4707 asks the team to weigh the argument that a newly created single-member district will make the coming election more competitive.

answer.exemplar: The argument is partly sound and partly not, and the team should say which part it is. A single-member district does raise the effective threshold for winning a seat, because a party needs a plurality in one area rather than a dispersed share across many, so in fragmented systems it can advantage the largest organised party rather than increase competition. What it does not do is make the vote itself more decisive: with three or four parties splitting the constituency more evenly, a first-past-the-post seat can still fall to a party with well under a third of the vote, and each vote carries more weight per seat, so the district is described as having a high magnitude of dispersion. The honest conclusion is that the change alters the effective threshold and the consequences of vote splitting, which must be modelled before anyone can claim the district will be more competitive.

questions.explanation: A single-member seat raises the effective threshold, which in fragmented systems can favour the largest party. The tempting claim confuses a higher entry barrier with a clearer outcome.
questions.hint: Separate the entry barrier from the clarity of the result.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the primary purpose of a get-out-the-vote campaign
questions.stem: Ticket VMB-5009 asks the team to state what a get-out-the-vote campaign primarily attempts to achieve.

answer.exemplar: A turnout drive converts intention into actual voting among people who have already told the party, or are reliably associated with it, that they intend to vote. It works through reminders about the practicalities of polling day, the offer of a lift or a polling station nearby, and the removal of small obstacles such as not knowing where to vote or how to complete the form. The object is not persuasion of undecided voters, which belongs to the campaign proper, and it is not registration, which belongs to the roll-building stage. A turnout operation that succeeds is one in which supporters who had intended to vote actually cast a ballot, and its results are usually reported as the number of votes that would otherwise have been lost.

questions.explanation: A turnout drive converts intention into actual voting among existing supporters. The distractors confuse it with persuasion, registration and leader visibility, which are separate tasks.
questions.hint: Think about the gap between intention and turnout.

options.text: Issue the fine only after polling day, so citizens do not feel targeted before they have voted.
options.misconception: delays the penalty instead of reducing the deterrent effect

options.text: Set the fine at a level that rises with the citizen's income, so the penalty is affordable to everyone.
options.misconception: assumes an income-linked fine is affordable to everyone

options.text: Let political parties collect the fine for the state, so the burden falls on the better resourced.
options.misconception: makes parties the collection agent for the penalty

options.text: Set the fine at a small uniform amount and provide a simple, prompt exemption for hardship and caring duties.

questions.explanation: A deterrent must not price out the citizens whose participation is most needed, so a small fine with a hardship exemption works best. The distractors delay, charge by income or privatise the penalty.
questions.hint: Ask who the penalty would deter most.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess what professional associations gain from backing parties
questions.stem: Ticket PIG-5403 asks the team to assess the claim that professional associations gain more from party funding than they contribute.

options.text: The claim is doubtful, because parties value a professional body's endorsement for its credibility.
The claim is doubtful, because associations usually finance parties rather than the other way round.
options.misconception: reverses the usual direction of the funding flow

options.text: The claim is sound, because parties collapse without professional associations' financial support.
options.misconception: claims parties depend on association funding

options.text: The claim is sound, because endorsements from professional bodies always decide close elections.
options.misconception: claims endorsements always decide close elections

questions.explanation: Associations contribute credibility and networks rather than cash, which is why parties prize their endorsements. The distractors reverse the funding direction and treat endorsements as decisive.
questions.hint: Consider what an association actually supplies.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Weigh a proposal for unedited full-length candidate interviews
questions.stem: Ticket MDE-5508 asks the team to weigh a proposal that all televised candidate interviews be aired unedited and in full.

options.text: The proposal is unwise, because unedited interviews always favour the most aggressive speakers.
options.misconception: assumes unedited broadcasts favour aggressive speakers

options.text: The proposal is unwise, because voters lose interest once a conversation runs beyond a few minutes.
options.misconception: assumes voters cannot tolerate long exchanges

options.text: The proposal is reasonable, because unedited full-length broadcasts limit the editor's power over the record.
The proposal is reasonable, because unedited interviews guarantee that every candidate is treated fairly.
options.misconception: believes unedited format guarantees equal treatment

questions.explanation: Full unedited broadcasts reduce gatekeeper discretion, which is the reform's purpose, but do not guarantee equal coverage. The distractors substitute claims about speakers and attention spans.
questions.hint: Ask what discretion the reform actually removes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the claim that a runoff lets voters correct a first-round mistake
questions.stem: Ticket ROF-5601 asks the team to evaluate the argument that a runoff gives voters a second chance to correct a first-round mistake.

answer.exemplar: The argument is only half true, and the team should say which half holds. It is true that a runoff lets voters reweigh their options: seeing a candidate eliminated can release a second preference that the first round concealed, and the final choice is made with fuller information about who is viable. It is false that a runoff is a general safety net, because a vote cast for a candidate who reaches the final cannot be transferred, so a voter's earlier decision may lock them into a candidate they later regret, and a plurality-first-round system can hand the runoff to a party that won the first round on a minority share. The defensible position is that runoffs improve information and moderate preferences, while adding a residual risk of entrenchment.

questions.explanation: Runoffs let voters react to the first-round outcome and release second preferences. The tempting claim that they correct mistakes overlooks that first-round votes cannot be transferred.
questions.hint: Check whether a first-round vote can still be changed.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the measure describing votes needed to win a seat
questions.stem: Ticket DST-5705 asks the team to identify the measure commonly used to describe how many votes a party needs to win a seat.

options.text: The effective threshold, which counts the votes needed to reach a seat in that district.
The national swing of two and a half per cent, which applies to every seat in the country.
options.misconception: confuses a uniform national swing with a seat threshold

options.text: The turnout of the previous election held in the same district.
options.misconception: uses past turnout as a measure of the votes needed

options.text: The number of registered voters in the constituency, which sets the majority mark.
options.misconception: treats the electorate size as the majority requirement

questions.explanation: The effective threshold expresses how many votes are needed to win a seat, given how votes convert into seats locally. The distractors substitute a national swing, past turnout and electorate size.
questions.hint: Think about votes needed, not votes cast.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why observers publish findings before the final result
questions.stem: Ticket EMN-5802 asks the team to explain why observers publish their findings before the final result is announced.

options.text: Because early publication increases the chance that observers will be invited back for the next poll.
options.misconception: assumes early publication secures future appointments

options.text: Because publication before the result allows observers to correct any errors in the count themselves.
options.misconception: claims observers can amend the official count

options.text: Because publication while the count is still open can prompt a review of problems that remain fixable.
Because only early findings qualify for inclusion in the official report of the commission.
options.misconception: invents a rule limiting official reports to early findings

questions.explanation: Publishing early gives problems a chance to be addressed while the count is still open. The distractors assume career advantage, a power to amend results and a non-existent reporting rule.
questions.hint: Think about what can still change at that moment.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Infer what coalition members are rewarding from their feedback

stimulus.body: The two parties disagreed on two matters. On the first, a date for closing a legacy facility, the smaller party could not get its preferred date accepted and had earlier told its members the date would be secured. On the second, the budget for a regional fund, it received more than it had expected. The smaller party's own members wrote to the larger party praising the budget outcome and asking what had happened over the facility date.

questions.stem: Ticket BAR-5907 asks the team to work out what the smaller party's members appear to be rewarding.

options.text: They are rewarding the larger party for refusing to make concessions on either of the two matters.
options.misconception: reads the messages as reward for inflexibility

options.text: They are rewarding the tangible gain on the fund while discounting the earlier promise about the date.
They are rewarding the larger party for honouring the facility date in exchange for the larger budget.
options.misconception: assumes the date was honoured in the bargain

options.text: They are rewarding the larger party for allowing the smaller party to set the budget figure itself.
options.misconception: infers the smaller party dictated the budget figure

questions.explanation: Members reward the visible gain and discount the unfulfilled promise, which fits how constituents score a deal. The distractors read the messages as praise for stubbornness or for a date not kept.
questions.hint: Watch which outcome the members name first.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the claim that a strong result removes the need for organisation
questions.stem: Ticket VMS-6001 asks the team to evaluate the claim that a strong election result removes the need for campaign organisation.

options.text: The claim is sound, because victory gives the party money and volunteers for future contests.
options.misconception: treats past victory as a substitute for organisation

options.text: The claim is sound, because turnout is highest in the election immediately after a large win.
options.misconception: asserts turnout peaks right after a win

options.text: The claim is unsound, because campaign organisation matters more in close contests than in safe ones.
options.misconception: says organisation matters more in close seats

options.text: The claim is unsound, because each cycle's organisation determines who is on the roll and who is contacted.

questions.explanation: Each cycle resets the electorate and voluntary effort, so organisation must be rebuilt every time. The distractors treat a win as a subsidy and confine organisation to close seats.
questions.hint: Think about what each new cycle resets.
